@Brian_Bolli My intention is to also retrofit these $30 Chinese Weigand door controllers so they are actually secure using Orange Pi Zero and SSH. All you need is the serial number of the door (1,2,3,4,etc) and wifi/net to pop them open. Plug the door controller into the camera via serial.

https://x.com/Brian_Bolli/status/1196907585519210497

1196945450508660737.a: @Brian_Bolli That also allows the camera to snap a photo when a card is swiped. Admin UI uses DLL wrapper around the RS-485 DLL to enable Ethernet. They use RS-485 over TCP or UDP IP Broadcast (0.0.0.255) with no security!!! It would be easy to wrap the RS-485 port in a SSH tunnel with certs.

1196946209774198784.a: @Brian_Bolli There are campuses with like 50,000 doors on these completely insecure systems and they often place them on the same LANs as wifi. Instead of ripping out 50,000 doors one could unplug Ethernet from the door controller, plug into Orange Pi plugged into the "vestigial" RS-485 port.

1196946823132397568.a: @Brian_Bolli And there are large US companies selling these things under their own brand names. I've been able to buy $30 generic "standards based" controllers from Alibaba and use them with the fancy US software from expensive brands. They all use the same protocols which have zero security.

1196947929438834689.a: @Brian_Bolli I had a few good days some months ago and was able to do a hardware debugging on some boards. I slapped together a camera that talked to the door over serial, replaced its Ethernet for proof of concept. It needs to support ONVIF to make it compatible with actual security systems.

1196948346453270529.a: @Brian_Bolli tldr; no one wants to do the work to implement ONVIF protocols properly on cheap door controllers and cameras. Clearly this was recognized as a problem and ONVIF seems to have been developed to solve it. It's not the hardware's fault. It's crap firmware.

1196949407691943937.a: @Brian_Bolli My proof of concept just setup netcat on the same port to the door's onboard TTL-serial with IP filters to control access. I mean, even just that tiny modicum of security makes the door vastly more secure; you at least have to guess/snoop the admin IP address and masquerade as it

1196950320091451393.a: @Brian_Bolli The admin software still works with the Orange Pi acting as a mediator in that way. The software just has to be told the IP of each door explicitly. Normally it broadcasts to 0.0.0.255 and each door decides if it will execute the command. (Broadcast could have 5 doors with 1 ID!)

1196950647909879814.a: @Brian_Bolli The admin software itself has users with passwords and gives the illusion of security. I imagine most people have no idea the doors are all wide open to anyone on the network.
